claim: A crucial evolutionary change in vertebrate history was the Palaeozoic (Devonian 419–359 million years ago) water-to-land transition.

evidence: This is stated as established scientific knowledge about vertebrate evolution.

claim: The primitive state of vertebrate lungs was unpaired.

source: Although some authors suggest that L. chalumnae fatty organ evidences a paired lung, previous studies proved that this organ is not the second lung, since there is no opened connection between this organ and the foregut or lung, nor lung plates surrounding it (Cupello et al., 2015; Cupello et al., 2017a; Cupello et al., 2017b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Cupello et al., 2015, 2017a, and 2017b.

claim: The paired condition of coelacanth lungs can be excluded.
source: Based on these, the paired condition of coelacanth lungs can be excluded.
evidence: This is an inference based on the evidence presented about coelacanth lung anatomy.

claim: The first developmental stage with lung anlage in Neoceratodus forsteri registered in this study is an early larva of 13.5 mm TL, with an unpaired morphology.
source: The first developmental stage with lung anlage registered in this study is an early larva of 13.5 mm TL, with an unpaired morphology represented primarily by lung anterior projection (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is based on direct observations from the developmental series and supported by Figure 4B.

claim: In Neoceratodus forsteri larvae of 16 mm, 17 mm, and 17.5 mm TL, a long and unpaired lung anlage is clearly identifiable and arises as a ventral depression of the post-pharyngeal foregut.
source: In larvae of 16 mm, 17 mm, and 17.5 mm TL, although organogenesis is still not complete, a long and unpaired lung anlage is clearly identifiable and arises as a ventral depression of the post-pharyngeal foregut (Figure 6E and F).
evidence: This is based on direct observations from the developmental series and supported by Figure 6E and F.

claim: In the 19 mm TL specimen of Neoceratodus forsteri, the unpaired lung starts its dorsal turn up in relation to the dorsal portion of the foregut.
source: In the 19 mm TL specimen, the unpaired lung starts its dorsal turn up in relation to the dorsal portion of the foregut (including the stomach) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on direct observations from the developmental series and supported by Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: In Neoceratodus forsteri, from 20.5 mm TL onward, organogenesis is completed.
source: From 20.5 mm TL onward, organogenesis is completed.
evidence: This is based on direct observations from the developmental series.

claim: In the larva of 20.5 mm TL of Neoceratodus forsteri, the lung remains unpaired and is ventrally connected to the post-pharyngeal foregut by a ventral, opened and long pneumatic duct.
source: In the larva of 20.5 mm TL, the lung remains unpaired and is ventrally connected to the post-pharyngeal foregut by a ventral, opened and long pneumatic duct.
evidence: This is based on direct observations from the developmental series.

claim: Air-breathing begins in Neoceratodus forsteri at 25 mm TL larval stage.
source: According to previous studies (Kemp, 1982; Kemp, 1986), air-breathing begins in N. forsteri at 25 mm TL larval stage.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kemp, 1982 and Kemp, 1986.

claim: The larva with 26.5 mm TL of Neoceratodus forsteri presents a lung wall slightly pleated.
source: Our results reveal that the larva with 26.5 mm TL presents a lung wall slightly pleated.
evidence: This is based on direct observations from the developmental series.

claim: From 50 mm TL larval stage onward in Neoceratodus forsteri, the lung wall is pleated eventually providing a high degree of alveolation.
source: From 50 mm TL larval stage onward, the lung wall is pleated eventually providing a high degree of alveolation.
evidence: This is based on direct observations from the developmental series.

claim: In the adult individual with 200 mm TL of Neoceratodus forsteri, the single lung displays internally two lateral chambers that are connected to a principal median chamber at both sides as a single structure.
source: In the adult individual with 200 mm TL, the single lung displays internally two lateral chambers that are connected to a principal median chamber at both sides as a single structure (Figure 4C–E).
evidence: This is based on direct observations from the developmental series and supported by Figure 4C–E.

claim: In adult specimens of Neoceratodus forsteri, the lung is highly compartmentalized by septa of smooth muscle and non-elastic connective tissue, as well as spongy alveolar structures.
source: In adult specimens of N. forsteri, the lung is highly compartmentalized by septa of smooth muscle and non-elastic connective tissue, as well as spongy alveolar structures (Grigg, 1965).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Grigg, 1965.

claim: In adult Neoceratodus forsteri, the lung makes a complete dorsal turn-up at its posterior portion in relation to the gastrointestinal tract.
source: At this developmental stage, the lung makes a complete dorsal turn-up at its posterior portion in relation to the gastrointestinal tract (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is based on direct observations from the developmental series and supported by Figure 4C.

claim: Some authors pointed to the presence of a second bud at the early developmental stages of Neoceratodus forsteri, referred as the left lung.
source: Although some authors pointed the presence of a second bud at the early developmental stages of N. forsteri, referred as the left lung (Spencer, 1893; Neumayer, 1904), the results presented here show an indubitably unpaired configuration for Neoceratodus lung throughout the ontogeny (Figures 4A–E–6E and F and Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Spencer, 1893 and Neumayer, 1904.

claim: The results presented here show an indubitably unpaired configuration for Neoceratodus lung throughout the ontogeny.
source: Although some authors pointed the presence of a second bud at the early developmental stages of N. forsteri, referred as the left lung (Spencer, 1893; Neumayer, 1904), the results presented here show an indubitably unpaired configuration for Neoceratodus lung throughout the ontogeny (Figures 4A–E–6E and F and Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on direct observations from the developmental series and supported by multiple figures.

claim: In Lepidosiren paradoxa, left and right tubes do not arise simultaneously.
source: Lungs of the four specimens studied here, from larva to adults (larva with 46 mm TL, juveniles with 68 mm TL and 222.1 mm TL, and adult with 400 mm TL), display a similar morphology, and surprisingly, left and right tubes do not arise simultaneously.
evidence: This is based on direct observations from the developmental series.

claim: In Lepidosiren paradoxa, only the right sac is connected to the pharynx by a long pneumatic duct.
source: Only the right sac is connected to the pharynx by a long pneumatic duct (Figure 6G and H and Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is based on direct observations from the developmental series and supported by figures.

claim: In Lepidosiren paradoxa, the left sac is a branch of the right one, connected by a posterior and secondary opening at the lung level.
source: The left sac is a branch of the right one, connected by a posterior and secondary opening at the lung level, already in dorsal position in relation to the foregut (Figure 6G and H and Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is based on direct observations from the developmental series and supported by figures.

claim: In Lepidosiren paradoxa, there is no connection of the left sac with the pneumatic duct.
source: There is no connection of the left sac with the pneumatic duct.
evidence: This is based on direct observations from the developmental series.

claim: In Lepidosiren paradoxa, only the pneumatic duct is ventrally positioned.
source: In L. paradoxa, only the pneumatic duct is ventrally positioned, and the lung makes a complete dorsal turn up from the right side of the upper gastrointestinal tract (Figure 4F–K and Figure 4—figure supplement 3), just after the ventral connection to the pharynx.
evidence: This is based on direct observations from the developmental series and supported by figures.

claim: In Lepidosiren paradoxa, the lung makes a complete dorsal turn up from the right side of the upper gastrointestinal tract, just after the ventral connection to the pharynx.
source: In L. paradoxa, only the pneumatic duct is ventrally positioned, and the lung makes a complete dorsal turn up from the right side of the upper gastrointestinal tract (Figure 4F–K and Figure 4—figure supplement 3), just after the ventral connection to the pharynx.
evidence: This is based on direct observations from the developmental series and supported by figures.

claim: This complete dorsal turn-up is also seen in the lung of adult specimens of Neoceratodus forsteri.
source: This complete dorsal turn-up is also seen in the lung of adult specimens of N. forsteri (Figure 4I–K).
evidence: This is based on direct observations and supported by Figure 4I–K.

claim: In Lepidosiren paradoxa, there are no anterior projections of the lung.
source: There are no anterior projections of the lung.
evidence: This is based on direct observations from the developmental series.

claim: Lung compartmentalization in Lepidosiren paradoxa is clearly observable through dissections, evidencing the high degree of alveolation.
source: Lung compartmentalization is clearly observable through dissections, evidencing the high degree of alveolation (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is based on direct observations from dissections and supported by Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: The lung of Lepidosiren paradoxa is remarkably similar to Polypterus senegalus lung.
source: Our results indicate that the lung of L. paradoxa is, in fact, remarkably similar to P. senegalus lung.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparative observations from the developmental series.

claim: The so-called left lung of Lepidosiren paradoxa is most likely a diverticulum or a modified lateral lobe.
source: The so-called left lung of L. paradoxa is most likely a diverticulum or a modified lateral lobe, which might have evolved secondarily, an advantage for enlarging the surface area for oxygen-uptake, eventually enabling the obligatory air-breathing performance in the linage towards L. paradoxa.
evidence: This is an inference based on the anatomical observations.

claim: The so-called left lung of Lepidosiren paradoxa might have evolved secondarily as an advantage for enlarging the surface area for oxygen-uptake.
source: The so-called left lung of L. paradoxa is most likely a diverticulum or a modified lateral lobe, which might have evolved secondarily, an advantage for enlarging the surface area for oxygen-uptake, eventually enabling the obligatory air-breathing performance in the linage towards L. paradoxa.
evidence: This is speculation about the evolutionary advantage of the anatomical feature.

claim: The modified lateral lobe of Lepidosiren paradoxa eventually enabled the obligatory air-breathing performance in the lineage towards L. paradoxa.
source: The so-called left lung of L. paradoxa is most likely a diverticulum or a modified lateral lobe, which might have evolved secondarily, an advantage for enlarging the surface area for oxygen-uptake, eventually enabling the obligatory air-breathing performance in the linage towards L. paradoxa.
evidence: This is speculation about the functional consequence of the anatomical feature.

claim: In early larvae of Salamandra salamandra with 35.5 mm TL and 42.8 mm TL, paired lungs are collapsed in its middle and posterior portion.
source: In early larvae with 35.5 mm TL and 42.8 mm TL, paired lungs are collapsed in its middle and posterior portion (Figure 5A and B).
evidence: This is based on direct observations from the developmental series and supported by Figure 5A and B.

claim: In early larvae of Salamandra salamandra, the internal lung wall is thin and smooth, without compartmentalization and/or alveolation in its inner wall.
source: The internal lung wall is thin and smooth, without compartmentalization and/or alveolation in its inner wall (Figure 6J and Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on direct observations from the developmental series and supported by figures.

claim: In Salamandra salamandra, from the early larvae onward, the muscular glottis develops on the ventral portion of the pharynx.
source: From the early larvae onward, the muscular glottis develops on the ventral portion of the pharynx, and both left and right lungs arise simultaneously and symmetrically from a long trachea and paired first order bronchioles (Figures 5C, D, 6I and J and Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on direct observations from the developmental series and supported by figures.

claim: In Salamandra salamandra, both left and right lungs arise simultaneously and symmetrically from a long trachea and paired first order bronchioles.
source: From the early larvae onward, the muscular glottis develops on the ventral portion of the pharynx, and both left and right lungs arise simultaneously and symmetrically from a long trachea and paired first order bronchioles (Figures 5C, D, 6I and J and Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on direct observations from the developmental series and supported by figures.

claim: In Salamandra salamandra, lungs are symmetrical in size and morphology and are placed in the anteriormost portion of the abdominal cavity.
source: Lungs are symmetrical in size and morphology and are placed in the anteriormost portion of the abdominal cavity, as described for other tetrapods (Figure 5C and D).
evidence: This is based on direct observations from the developmental series and supported by Figure 5C and D.

claim: In postmetamorphic juveniles of Salamandra salamandra (of 81.85 mm TL), paired lungs are already functional, not collapsed, and the main organ for oxygen-uptake.
source: In postmetamorphic juveniles (of 81.85 mm TL), paired lungs are already functional, not collapsed, and the main organ for oxygen-uptake (Goniakowska-Witalińska, 1978; Goniakowska-Witalińska, 1982).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Goniakowska-Witalińska, 1978 and 1982.

claim: In Salamandra salamandra, from postmetamorphic juveniles onward, lungs are highly compartmentalized by multiple septa.
source: From this developmental stage onward, lungs are highly compartmentalized by multiple septa.
evidence: This is based on direct observations from the developmental series.

claim: Due to the paired and compartmentalized anatomy, the lung surface area for oxygen-uptake, as well as its volume capacity, increase substantially in Salamandra salamandra.
source: Due to the paired and compartmentalized anatomy, the lung surface area for oxygen-uptake, as well as its volume capacity, increase substantially – both important features for a functional lung in dry environments.
evidence: This is an inference based on the anatomical observations.

claim: Increased lung surface area and volume capacity are important features for a functional lung in dry environments.
source: Due to the paired and compartmentalized anatomy, the lung surface area for oxygen-uptake, as well as its volume capacity, increase substantially – both important features for a functional lung in dry environments.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about lung function.

claim: At different developmental stages of Salamandra salamandra, lungs are truly paired since both left and right lungs arise simultaneously and symmetrically and are directly connected to the trachea.
source: Here we confirm that at different developmental stages of S. salamandra, lungs are truly paired since both left and right lungs arise simultaneously and symmetrically and are directly connected to the trachea.
evidence: This is based on direct observations from the developmental series.

claim: Throughout the ontogeny, Salamandra salamandra lungs have a ventral origin, and make a partial dorsal turn-up in its posterior portion, remaining parallel to the dorsal wall of the upper gastrointestinal tract.
source: Throughout the ontogeny, S. salamandra lungs have a ventral origin, and makes a partial dorsal turn-up in its posterior portion, remaining parallel to the dorsal wall of the upper gastrointestinal tract.
evidence: This is based on direct observations from the developmental series.

claim: Due to the rarity of soft tissue preservation in the fossil record, only one species of salamandrid, Phosphotriton sigei, presents its lung preserved.
source: Due to the rarity of soft tissue preservation in the fossil record, only one species of salamandrid, Phosphotriton sigei presents its lung preserved (Tissier et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Tissier et al., 2017.

claim: The lung of Phosphotriton sigei is described as multichambered, placed in the anteriormost part of the abdominal cavity.
source: This lung is described as multichambered, placed in the anteriormost part of the abdominal cavity (Tissier et al., 2017), such as in the living salamandrid described above.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Tissier et al., 2017.

claim: Vertebrate lungs are traditionally defined as ventral paired organs derived from the ventral portion of the posterior pharynx or post-pharyngeal foregut.
source: Traditionally, vertebrate lungs are defined as ventral paired organs derived from the ventral portion of the posterior pharynx or post-pharyngeal foregut (Perry et al., 2001; Funk et al., 2020; Lambertz et al., 2015; Graham, 1997; Kardong, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Perry et al., 2001, Funk et al., 2020, Lambertz et al., 2015, Graham, 1997, and Kardong, 2015.

claim: This study demonstrates the presence of an unambiguous unpaired lung that develops from the ventral foregut in osteichthyan fishes.
source: However, we demonstrate here the presence of an unambiguous unpaired lung, that develops from the ventral foregut, but sometimes occupy the dorsal position later in the development of osteichthyan fishes (Figure 7).
evidence: This is based on the data presented in the manuscript and supported by Figure 7.

claim: The unpaired lung sometimes occupies the dorsal position later in the development of osteichthyan fishes.
source: However, we demonstrate here the presence of an unambiguous unpaired lung, that develops from the ventral foregut, but sometimes occupy the dorsal position later in the development of osteichthyan fishes (Figure 7).
evidence: This is based on the data presented in the manuscript and supported by Figure 7.

claim: True paired lungs are stated when bilateral lung buds arise simultaneously and are both connected directly to the foregut.
source: Based on our results, true paired lungs are stated when bilateral lung buds arise simultaneously and are both connected directly to the foregut, as observed in the salamander (Figures 5B, D, 7).
evidence: This is a new definition proposed based on the data presented in the manuscript.

claim: All living actinopterygian and sarcopterygian fishes have unpaired lungs.
source: The sister group to all other living actinopterygian (polypterids) and all living sarcopterygian fishes have a clearly unpaired lung in early developmental stages (Figure 1B) that can be developed in later stages either in a unilobed or a secondarily multilobed lung (Figures 1D–F ,–7), but not in a true paired lung.
evidence: This is based on the data presented in the manuscript and supported by figures.

claim: Polypterus senegalus and the lungfish Lepidosiren paradoxa possess secondary multilobed structure from the larval stage onward since the lung is derived from a unilateral connection to the foregut.
source: P. senegalus and the lungfish L. paradoxa possess secondary multilobed structure from the larval stage onward since the lung is derived from a unilateral connection to the foregut (Figure 4G, H, J and K).
evidence: This is based on the data presented in the manuscript and supported by figures.

claim: The presence of secondary multilobed morphology likely represents an advantage for the obligatory air-breathing behavior of Polypterus senegalus and Lepidosiren paradoxa, raising the respiratory compliance.
source: The presence of this secondary multilobed morphology likely represents an advantage for the obligatory air-breathing behavior of these taxa, raising the respiratory compliance.
evidence: This is speculation about the functional advantage of the anatomical feature.

claim: In the teleost Batrachomoeus trispinosus, the non-respiratory gas bladder is described as paired.
source: In the teleost Batrachomoeus trispinosus, the non-respiratory gas bladder is also described as paired (Rice and Bass, 2009), although it is most probably a secondary condition.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Rice and Bass, 2009.

claim: The paired gas bladder in Batrachomoeus trispinosus is most probably a secondary condition.
source: In the teleost Batrachomoeus trispinosus, the non-respiratory gas bladder is also described as paired (Rice and Bass, 2009), although it is most probably a secondary condition.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparative data.

claim: The most parsimonious scenario inferred from the data mapped on the phylogenetic framework is that the vertebrate lung was unpaired at the evolutionary origin.
source: The most parsimonious scenario inferred from our data mapped on the phylogenetic framework (Figure 7) is that the vertebrate lung was unpaired at the evolutionary origin.
evidence: This is an inference based on the data presented in the manuscript and phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 7.

claim: Living lunged osteichthyans are key taxa for the understanding of how evolutionary constraints shaped breathing adaptations on land.
source: Since soft tissues are rarely preserved in fossils, living lunged osteichthyans are key taxa for the understanding of how evolutionary constraints shaped breathing adaptations on land.
evidence: This is an inference based on the rarity of fossil soft tissue preservation.

claim: The ancestral condition of the lung is a median unpaired organ.
source: Our study suggests that the ancestral condition of the lung is a median unpaired organ (Figure 7), thereby being inconsistent with the scenario that the lung evolved through a modification of the posteriormost pharyngeal pouch assumed to be present in primitive taxa (Kastschenko, 1887; Goodrich, 1931).
evidence: This is an inference based on the data presented in the manuscript and supported by Figure 7.

claim: The finding that the ancestral condition of the lung is unpaired is inconsistent with the scenario that the lung evolved through a modification of the posteriormost pharyngeal pouch.
source: Our study suggests that the ancestral condition of the lung is a median unpaired organ (Figure 7), thereby being inconsistent with the scenario that the lung evolved through a modification of the posteriormost pharyngeal pouch assumed to be present in primitive taxa (Kastschenko, 1887; Goodrich, 1931).
evidence: This is an inference based on the data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The evolutionary origin of the lung was likely independent of the pharyngeal pouch at the morphological level.
source: Consequently, the evolutionary origin of the lung was likely independent of the pharyngeal pouch at the morphological level.
evidence: This is an inference based on the finding that the ancestral lung was unpaired.

claim: The vertebrate lung is either an unpaired or paired respiratory organ developing ventrally from the foregut.
source: From this evolutionary point of view, our results lead to a new definition of the vertebrate lung: either an unpaired or paired respiratory organ developing ventrally from the foregut.
evidence: This is a new definition proposed based on the data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Vestigial forms secondarily released from the respiratory function should be also designated as lungs.
source: Vestigial forms secondarily released from the respiratory function should be also designated as lungs (e.g. the lung of coelacanths).
evidence: This is a proposed criterion for defining lungs.

claim: Some criteria previously used for discriminating lungs from gas bladders are no longer supported, including paired/unpaired organization and position ventral to the alimentary tract.
source: Some criteria previously used for discriminating lungs from gas bladders are no longer supported, including: paired/unpaired organization, position ventral to the alimentary tract (Marcus, 1937; Funk et al., 2020; Lambertz et al., 2015; Graham, 1997), as well as its function.
evidence: This is an inference based on the data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Function is no longer a supported criterion for discriminating lungs from gas bladders.
source: Some criteria previously used for discriminating lungs from gas bladders are no longer supported, including: paired/unpaired organization, position ventral to the alimentary tract (Marcus, 1937; Funk et al., 2020; Lambertz et al., 2015; Graham, 1997), as well as its function.
evidence: This is an inference based on the data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The only morphological characteristic that can be used to distinguish lungs and gas bladders is the ventral and dorsal origins from the foregut, respectively.
source: Actually, the only morphological characteristic that can be used to distinguish lungs and gas bladders is the ventral and dorsal origins from the foregut, respectively (Funk et al., 2020; Cass et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Funk et al., 2020 and Cass et al., 2013.

claim: The dorsal position of the majority of osteichthyans lungs may be related to its dual and secondary functionality of respiration and buoyancy control.
source: The dorsal position of the majority of osteichthyans lungs described here may be related to its dual and secondary functionality of respiration and buoyancy control (Thomson, 1968).
evidence: This is speculation supported by citation to Thomson, 1968.

claim: The phenotypic differentiation into true paired lungs in tetrapods may be related to differential gene expressions.
source: This phenotypic differentiation into true paired lungs in tetrapods may be related to differential gene expressions (Funk et al., 2020; Bi et al., 2021).
evidence: This is speculation supported by citations to Funk et al., 2020 and Bi et al., 2021.

claim: At a level of developmental mechanism, the possibility of co-options of gene regulatory networks of the pharyngeal pouch morphogenesis cannot be excluded.
source: Nevertheless, at a level of developmental mechanism, the possibility of co-options of gene regulatory networks of the pharyngeal pouch morphogenesis cannot be excluded, as both the lung bud and pharyngeal pouch develop through the invagination of the foregut endoderm.
evidence: This is speculation about possible developmental mechanisms.

claim: Both the lung bud and pharyngeal pouch develop through the invagination of the foregut endoderm.
source: Nevertheless, at a level of developmental mechanism, the possibility of co-options of gene regulatory networks of the pharyngeal pouch morphogenesis cannot be excluded, as both the lung bud and pharyngeal pouch develop through the invagination of the foregut endoderm.
evidence: This is stated as established embryological knowledge.

claim: Bifurcation morphogenesis into true paired lungs was not developed yet in osteichthyan fish ancestors.
source: According to morphological evidence presented here, bifurcation morphogenesis into true paired lungs was not developed yet in osteichthyan fish ancestors.
evidence: This is an inference based on the data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Based on the extant phylogenetic bracket, the bilaterally paired nature of the lung evolved only in the lineage towards fossil and extant tetrapods, as a synapomorphy of this clade.
source: Based on the extant phylogenetic bracket, we infer that the bilaterally paired nature of the lung evolved only in the lineage towards fossil and extant tetrapods, as a synapomorphy of this clade (Figures 5 and 7).
evidence: This is an inference based on the data presented in the manuscript and supported by figures.

claim: The morphological modification to paired lungs brought about improvement of the efficiency in oxygen-uptake from the air.
source: This morphological modification brought about improvement of the efficiency in oxygen-uptake from the air, as the paired lungs having parallel air flows exchange the air more quickly than the unpaired lung having only single air flow does.
evidence: This is an inference about the functional consequence of paired lungs.

claim: Paired lungs having parallel air flows exchange the air more quickly than the unpaired lung having only single air flow.
source: This morphological modification brought about improvement of the efficiency in oxygen-uptake from the air, as the paired lungs having parallel air flows exchange the air more quickly than the unpaired lung having only single air flow does.
evidence: This is stated as a functional explanation for the advantage of paired lungs.

claim: The innovation of paired lungs led to the elevation of metabolic rate that was required for the sustained body support against the gravity.
source: This innovation led to the elevation of metabolic rate that was required for the sustained body support against the gravity.
evidence: This is an inference about the physiological consequence of paired lungs.

claim: Paired lungs may have been present also in early tetrapods.
source: Paired lungs may have been present also in early tetrapods and were probably essential to raise lung surface area and volume capacity during the evolution of vertebrate respiratory system and the air-breathing intensification at the water-to-land transition.
evidence: This is speculation about the presence of paired lungs in early tetrapods.

claim: Paired lungs were probably essential to raise lung surface area and volume capacity during the evolution of vertebrate respiratory system and the air-breathing intensification at the water-to-land transition.
source: Paired lungs may have been present also in early tetrapods and were probably essential to raise lung surface area and volume capacity during the evolution of vertebrate respiratory system and the air-breathing intensification at the water-to-land transition.
evidence: This is speculation about the functional importance of paired lungs during the water-to-land transition.

claim: Salamanders are often considered to have retained plesiomorphic characteristics of tetrapod stance and locomotion.
source: As salamanders are often considered to have retained plesiomorphic characteristics of tetrapod stance and locomotion (Pierce et al., 2020), we used them here also as a model for understanding lung evolution in tetrapods.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Pierce et al., 2020.

claim: Salamandra salamandra was used as a model for understanding lung evolution in tetrapods.
source: As salamanders are often considered to have retained plesiomorphic characteristics of tetrapod stance and locomotion (Pierce et al., 2020), we used them here also as a model for understanding lung evolution in tetrapods.
evidence: This is stated as the rationale for including Salamandra salamandra in the study.

claim: Propagation phase-contrast microtomography was the unique way to study the anatomy and histology of embryos and larvae at micrometer scale.
source: Due to the extremely small size of the embryos and larvae, and to the weak density difference between soft tissues of the abdominal cavity, propagation phase-contrast microtomography was the unique way to study their anatomy and histology at micrometer scale.
evidence: This is stated as the methodological justification for using synchrotron x-ray microtomography.

claim: Phase-contrast microtomography is only achieved at synchrotron sources.
source: Phase-contrast microtomography being only achieved at synchrotron sources, we accessed the anatomy of these rare and tiny samples at the Synchrotron SOLEIL and Synchrotron SPring-8.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about the technology.

claim: The high brightness of the synchrotrons was essential for the material and enabled the collection of high resolution scans in short timescales.
source: The high brightness of the synchrotrons was essential for our material and enabled the collection high resolution scans in short timescales.
evidence: This is stated as the advantage of using synchrotron sources.
